readerTitle: Two good numbers from a café's loyalty card, and why neither proves it works
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 카페 스탬프 카드, 반려동물 용품점 적립 카드) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 좋아 보이는 실험 숫자는 먼저 '무엇 중에서의 비율인가'와 '평소 흔들림보다 큰가'를 물어본 뒤 믿는다.
misconception: 교환율이 높고 매출이 올랐으니 적립 카드는 효과가 있다.

sources.text: 비율의 분모와 표본 변동(신호 대 잡음)에 관한 기본 통계 개념

factChecks.note: 교환율 계산: 완성 카드 기준 45 ÷ 60 = 75%, 배포 카드 기준 45 ÷ 400 = 11.25%(약 11%). 카드 문구와 일치하는지 확인하세요.
반려동물 용품점: 교환자 20명 가정 시 90% = 18명. 수치는 피드백 설명용 가정입니다.

cards.title: Two good numbers from a café's loyalty card
body: Mina's café handed out 400 stamp cards: buy nine coffees, get the tenth free. Four weeks later her barista was thrilled. "75% of the cards were redeemed!"
Weekly sales were up about 4%, too. Two numbers, both good news. Both may be telling her much less than they seem.

image.label: A café counter with a stack of stamp cards and a sales printout
image.brief: 따뜻한 톤의 동네 카페 카운터. 도장이 찍힌 종이 스탬프 카드 더미와 매출 영수증 출력물. 바리스타가 웃으며 "75%!"라고 적힌 메모를 들고 있고, 사장은 고개를 갸웃. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Should Mina keep the card?
body: The free coffees cost Mina money, and the cards take staff time. Her barista reports: 75% of cards were redeemed, and weekly sales rose about 4% during the four-week test.
What should she do with these numbers?

options.text: Keep it. A 75% redemption rate and rising sales are clear proof
options.feedback: You get a quick decision, but you're trusting two numbers you haven't questioned. The 75% may not mean what it sounds like.

options.text: First ask what the 75% is out of, and whether 4% is bigger than a normal week's swing
options.feedback: Two quick questions before deciding. Each one checks a different way a good-looking number can fool you.

options.text: Drop it. Free coffees eat into margins no matter what
options.feedback: Cost matters, but you'd be ignoring the test entirely. The card might still pay off once you read it properly.

cards.title: 75% of what?
body: The barista divided by **completed cards**, not cards handed out. Counted against all 400 cards, only about 11% ended in a free coffee.

cards.eyebrow: Concept at work · Ratios and denominators
cards.title: The bottom number decides the story.
body: Both percentages are correct. They answer different questions. The 75% says people who fill a card usually claim the coffee. That's hardly surprising.
Mina's real question is whether the card brings people back more often. For that, the **denominator** has to be everyone who got a card, and the top number has to be visits, not prizes.

image.label: Funnel from 400 cards to 60 filled to 45 claimed
image.brief: 깔때기 인포그래픽. 위에서부터 "400 cards handed out", "60 filled", "45 claimed". 오른쪽에 두 개의 괄호로 "75% = 45 ÷ 60"과 "11% = 45 ÷ 400"을 나란히 표시. 분모 부분을 강조색으로.

cards.softwareNote: Apps hit the same trap with "90% retention among users who finished onboarding." Divide by everyone who signed up and the number can look very different.

cards.title: Is 4% more than a normal wobble?
body: Average weekly sales rose from $9,700 to $10,075, a gain of $375. But before the card, weeks already swung by up to $800 with no change at all.

cards.title: The lift is smaller than the usual swing. Now what?
body: The $375 gain sits inside the range of ordinary weeks. Weather, school holidays or a nearby event could explain it.

options.text: Call it a win. Sales went up, and that's what counts
options.feedback: This reads noise as signal. With four weeks and big natural swings, the bump could easily vanish next month.

options.text: Run it longer and track how often card holders visit compared with before
options.feedback: This separates signal from noise: more weeks shrink the role of luck, and visit counts measure what the card is meant to change.

options.text: Call it a failure. No clear lift means no effect
options.feedback: Fair caution, but a small sample can hide a real effect as easily as it can fake one. Unclear is not the same as zero.

cards.title: Better numbers still have limits.
body: Even with the right denominator, card holders may simply be Mina's regulars. They'd have come anyway, so their high visit counts can flatter the card.
And more weeks cost real money in free coffees. Set a stopping point in advance, such as eight more weeks, rather than testing until the answer you want shows up.

cards.title: Now it's a pet supply shop.
body: A shop starts a card: buy five bags of dog food, get the sixth free. After two weeks the manager reports: "90% of customers who redeemed bought again, and sales are up 6%." The owner wants to extend it to every product.

options.text: Extend it now. Both numbers are strong
options.feedback: Fast, but untested. Redeemers are the shop's most loyal buyers, and two weeks is too short to trust a 6% swing.

options.text: Ask how many people the 90% covers, and compare 6% with normal two-week swings
options.feedback: Both concepts at once. If only 20 people redeemed, 90% is 18 customers. And 6% means little if sales often move that much on their own.

options.text: Skip the numbers and ask customers if they like the card
options.feedback: Useful for ideas, but liking a card isn't the same as buying more. Fix the numbers rather than drop them.

cards.title: Before trusting a test, ask: out of what, and bigger than normal?
body: This lesson used two ideas. **Ratios and denominators:** check what's on the bottom of a percentage. **Signal vs noise:** compare a change with how much things move on their own.
**Try it today:** take one success number from your business. Write down its denominator and the biggest swing you've seen without any change.
